metadata.title: Machine-Learning Applications in Predicting Students’ Non-Cognitive Skills: Evidence from PISA 2022
metadata.venue: Fudan Journal of the Humanities and Social Sciences

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the publicly available PISA 2022 student dataset (15-year-olds) and constructs an analytic sample of N=75,217 after applying inclusion criteria tied to Module 8 and missingness rules. The manuscript does not report using PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or any replicate-weight scheme; therefore, the analysis is treated as unweighted. Missing responses were recoded as system missing and then dropped, which can interact with the PISA sampling design if weights are not applied. The paper also performs nested cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning, but it does not describe any weight-aware resampling or weighting inside the ML training pipeline.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variable is an equally weighted composite index of non-cognitive skills (NCS) built from Likert-scale items, rather than a PV-based cognitive achievement score. The paper also does not describe PV generation/combination procedures, consistent with a non-cognitive outcome. Missing data handling is reported as listwise deletion: observations with missing data across variables were dropped after recoding invalid/skipped/not applicable responses as system missing.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 student dataset and restricted to students who took Module 8 (non-cognitive skills). Recoded invalid, skipped, and not applicable responses as system missing. Dropped all observations with missing data. Additional inclusion criteria required: (1) participation in Module 8; (2) less than 10% missing data overall; (3) exclusion when the dependent variable (non-cognitive skills) was missing; and (4) exclusion when any factor in the independent groups (background characteristics, cognitive-motivational traits, cognitive performance indicators) had missing values. Final analytic sample comprised 75,217 students across the listed ten OECD countries/partner economies.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model: Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) — Test MSE: 0.2399 (mean across outer folds: 0.2399), Test R²: 0.3038 (mean across outer folds: 0.3038). Compared to Random Forest — Test MSE: 0.2447, Test R²: 0.2898; Lasso — Test MSE: 0.2529, Test R²: 0.2529.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Module 8) data on non-cognitive skills, the study leveraged sense of belonging, expected educational level, family support, 21st century mathematics efficacy, and mathematics proactive behavior to predict the non-cognitive skills composite, finding that Gradient Boosting Machine achieved the highest predictive accuracy (highest R² and lowest MSE among OLS, Lasso, and Random Forest). This indicates that interventions prioritizing cognitive-motivational supports (e.g., self-efficacy/efficacy and proactive behaviors) alongside belonging- and aspiration-building supports may be more effective for improving students’ non-cognitive development, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 student data (15-year-olds) restricted to Module 8 to predict a non-cognitive skills outcome defined as an equally weighted composite index across OECD non-cognitive domains. The analytic sample includes 75,217 students from ten OECD countries/partner economies (Australia, Spain, Estonia, Hong Kong, Ireland, Korea, Macao, Singapore, Chinese Taipei, Turkey). After recoding invalid/skipped/not applicable responses as missing, the authors applied listwise deletion and evaluated models using nested 5-fold cross-validation with hyperparameter tuning. Gradient Boosting Machine outperformed OLS, Lasso, and Random Forest, with test performance summarized by MSE ≈ 0.2399 and R² ≈ 0.3038 (vs. RF R² ≈ 0.2898; Lasso R² ≈ 0.2663). SHAP interpretation indicated cognitive-motivational traits as the most influential group, with several math-related beliefs/behaviors contributing positively or negatively. Limitations include cross-sectional prediction (no causal identification) and the absence of reported PISA survey-weight usage.
